extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; researchers concerned with correct scientific reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and avoid common a priori fallacies and natural prejudices that vitiate scientific inquiry (e.g., mistaking linguistic categories for natural kinds, assuming single causes, or deriving laws without experiment). The page enumerates and exemplifies these methodological errors with illustrations from history and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mysticism (attributing objective existence to mental creations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The misapprehension of general language that ascribes objective existence to the subjective creations of our own faculties — treating ideas or feelings of the mind as if they were distinct, immutable realities (e.g., Universal Substances, τὸ ὄν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating abstract general terms (like 'man', 'whiteness', 'being') as denoting independent external entities. Do not substitute contemplation of mental constructs for empirical investigation of the world. Example anti-patterns: positing 'universal man' as an entity distinct from individual persons; taking universals as the only proper subjects of science because they appear immutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of Sufficient Reason (a priori proofs of physical laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting that a phenomenon must follow a particular law because we see no reason why it should deviate (i.e., because no preference among alternatives is apparent), and thereby attempting to establish physical laws _a priori_.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that absence of an apparent reason for one alternative implies impossibility of others. Such reasoning can be petitio principii. Empirical evidence, not purely speculative balancing of alternatives, is the proper ground for establishing laws (examples: fallacious proofs of the law of inertia and the first law of motion). Prefer experiment and observation over a priori symmetry arguments that assume what must be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming linguistic distinctions map to natural distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudice that differences in nature must correspond to the distinctions and classes used in popular or common language — i.e., that the taxonomy of ordinary speech reveals natural kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical that categories suggested by everyday language are natural kinds relevant to scientific explanation. Test whether linguistic classes correspond to empirical regularities before treating them as scientific categories. Example: Greek philosophers trying to derive nature's classes from the forms of common language (Aristotle's analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of contrarieties (inferring natural oppositions from conceptual oppositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that adjectives or substances opposed in language or abstract thought must indicate a fundamental antithesis in nature (e.g., deducing physical doctrines from contrasts like Limited/Unlimited, Odd/Even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let binary or rhetorical oppositions drive claims about the natural world. Historical examples (Pythagorean-derived oppositions, Aristotle deducing four elements) show how such inferences can produce dogma rather than empirical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-cause assumption / denying plurality of causes (Baconian critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that a phenomenon has one invariable 'forma' or single cause present in all instances, and attempting to discover that one cause by exclusion, rather than allowing for multiple, varying causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many phenomena (especially sensible qualities) arise from a plurality of causes or conditions. Prefer investigations that determine the effects of given causes (effects-of-causes) rather than trying, by elimination, to find one unique cause of an effect. Example anti-pattern: Bacon's method tacitly presumes a single cause for heat, color, etc., leading to failure in fields where many contributing factors exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing conditions/causes with the phenomenon itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Using language and reasoning that treats the conditions or supposed causes of a phenomenon as if they are identical with the phenomenon (e.g., speaking as if heat itself were the particular motion presumed to be its condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear distinction between an effect (the phenomenon as experienced) and the conditions or mechanisms that produce it. Avoid linguistic slippage that equates the two. Example: Bacon and Darwin language that speaks of 'heat' or 'idea' as if they literally are certain motions or configurations, rather than effects dependent on such conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming causes resemble their effects (the 'like produces like' fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudice that the conditions or causes of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon itself, or that external resemblances indicate causal efficacy (includes the 'Doctrine of Signatures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer causal relations from superficial resemblance. Empirical testing is required to establish causation. Historical examples: medicinal uses inferred from resemblance (turmeric for jaundice, 'eye-bright' for eye complaints), belief that properties of elements must resemble properties of their compounds, and magical/ sympathetic practices (Medea's broths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming mental representations must resemble external objects (perception-by-idea fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that sensations or mental images produced in us by perception must closely copy or resemble the external object (e.g., Epicurean species, or modern idea-based theories treating perception as literal copies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require resemblance between perceptual effects and their external causes. Accept that sensations may bear no similarity to the cause; treat perception theories as empirical hypotheses to be examined rather than necessary truths. Example corrective: Reid's arguments showing sensations need not be copies of external objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving physical laws purely by geometric/a priori reasoning (avoiding empirical appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to establish the most general facts of the outward world by sophistical or purely a priori geometric reasoning without appeal to experiment (e.g., Archimedes' reliance on assumed balancing principles as if not drawn from experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat geometric or mathematical reasoning concerning the natural world as requiring empirical corroboration. Be cautious of methods that prefer a priori deduction from assumed symmetries or idealized premises over checking against observation and experiment.
